# Dr. Munindar P. Singh's Writing Guidelines — Complete Reference

This is the comprehensive reference for all writing, grammar, editing, and formatting rules from Dr. Singh's advice pages. Loaded on demand by the academic-writing skill.

**Sources:**
- https://www.csc2.ncsu.edu/faculty/mpsingh/local/advice/grammar.html
- https://www.csc2.ncsu.edu/faculty/mpsingh/local/advice/editing.html
- https://www.csc2.ncsu.edu/faculty/mpsingh/local/advice/spellings.html
- https://www.csc2.ncsu.edu/faculty/mpsingh/local/advice/writing.html

---

## 1. GRAMMAR BASICS

### Given-Then-New Structure
- First part of sentence: what is given/well-known
- Remaining part: what is being presented as new
- Examples:
  - "My students like pizza." Given: I have students; new: what they like
  - "What my students like is pizza." Given: they like something; new: it's pizza
  - "The ones who like pizza are my students." Given: some people like pizza; new: they're my students

### Active Voice
- Use active voice where possible (almost always)

### Personal Style
- Use "we" instead of "I" for authors
- Use "you" and "we" instead of "one"
- Over-use of pronouns can be tiresome; replace with neutral entities
  - "This paper develops..." instead of "We develop..."
  - "Section 3 shows..." instead of "In Section 3, we show..."

### Apostrophes
- Use for possessives/genitives, NOT for plurals
- Avoid "ETD's" when you mean multiple ETDs
- Use "ETD's" only for possession: "The ETD's link is broken"

### Distributive Properties
- Don't use plurals for distributive properties
- "each agent plays a role" NOT "agents play roles"
- One-to-one relationships are more informative than many-to-many

### Eliminate Unnecessary Text
- For any doubtful construction, check if eliminating it costs anything
- Text that can be deleted without loss of meaning should be deleted
- Sentences that give the most grief in phrasing are often not as essential as believed

### Minimize Pronouns
- Don't use more pronouns than needed: this, it, and others are often confusing
- Referring to something with a pronoun after a gap of a sentence or two is highly confusing
- If you can come up with names (for people, projects, approaches), write out the name each time

### Citations
- Use author names when citing: "Chopra [3] says..." or "Chopra [2022] says..."
- Don't say "The authors of [7] show..." — just name them
- "In [7], the authors show..." is wordy and meaningless

### Comparators
- Always specify comparison: "our approach is faster than X" NOT "our approach is faster"
- Use "than" not "as compared to"
- Don't use superlatives as comparators: NOT "fastest than X"
- Don't use meaningless statements: "this problem has received limited attention" — everything is "limited"

### Hyphens and Dashes
- Hyphens for compounds: "agent-based"
- En-dashes (--) for ranges: "10--15"
- Em-dashes (---) for parenthetical remarks
- Example: "agents---well-known for at least 10--15 years---have become popular"
- Use hyphens where compounds are modifiers: "run-time error" but "at run time"
- Also: "well-defined case" but "this case is well defined"
- Watch "low level" vs "low-level" and cousins
- Don't hyphenate when prefix isn't standalone: "redo" not "re-do"
  - Exception: ambiguity cases like "re-sent" vs "resent"

### Verb/Noun Forms
- "Set up" (verb) vs "setup" (noun): "You set up your experiment; what you end up with is a setup"
- "Feed back" (verb) vs "feedback" (noun): same pattern

### Number Ranges
- "2008--2015 is a range" ✓
- "over 2008--2015" ✓
- "between 2008 and 2015" ✓
- NOT "between 2008--2015" ✗
- NOT "from 2008--2015" ✗

### Tense for Paper Structure
- Don't use past/future for what's in the paper
- NOT "We have presented..." or "We will present..."
- USE "We present..." or "Section 5 presents..."

### Abbreviations and Conjunctions
- Write "e.g.," and "i.e.," with commas
- Never begin sentence with "E.g.," or "I.e.," or any abbreviation
- Don't use "however" to separate sentence-level clauses with comma
  - "I like pizza. However, it makes me sleepy." ✓
  - "I like pizza, however, it makes me sleepy." ✗
- Don't use "however" where "howsoever" is intended
  - "This agent can process sessions, howsoever many may be initiated."

### Commas and Semicolons
- "i.e." yields clause of same type: "My friend won; i.e., he got selected" ✓
- Subordinate clauses need closing comma: "A, which is a B, sends a message" ✓
- "Both types of agent, consumers and providers, may initiate a conversation." ✓
- Look out for spurious commas: NOT "the commitment, the buyer makes" ✗
- Commas separate subordinate clauses; semicolons separate independent clauses with main verbs

### That vs. Which
- "P that Q" = {x: P(x) and Q(x)} — restrictive
- "P, which Q" = {x: P(x)} and claims P entails Q — non-restrictive
- "large computers that are fast" = large AND fast computers
- "large computers, which are fast" = large computers (claiming they're all fast)

### Only Placement
- "can only be achieved by..." vs "can be achieved only by..." — very different meanings

### Perspective Consistency
- Don't switch perspective across sentences
- If one sentence says "fetching" a result, the next shouldn't say "returning" a result
- Decide which side you are on

### Don't Exaggerate
- If you say "several shortcomings," list several
- Otherwise say "some shortcomings" or "the following shortcomings"

### Read for Sound
- Watch for inadvertent phrases: "an agent advertises a good deal" — good deal of advertising or a deal that is good?
- Reread prose aloud to catch unintended double meanings

### Enumeration
- Don't precede with exact count: NOT "the following three points..."
- Counts go wrong when editing; better to omit

### "On the Other Hand"
- Only use "on the other hand" if preceded by "on the one hand"
- Better alternatives: "conversely," "in contrast," "by contrast"

### Shorter Constructs
- "there is a semantics for X" → "X has a semantics" (shorter, better)
- "The following are X that are Y" → "The following X are Y" (save two words!)

### Redundancy
- Avoid: "add additional slots", "linear lines", "choose among choices"
- "this box is blue in color" → "this box is blue"
- "business logic is proprietary in nature" → "business logic is proprietary"
- "Less number of" packs two errors in three words

### Set Constructions
- "Each of X..." means X is a plural set (must have ≥2 members)
- "One of X..." means X is a plural set (must have ≥2 members)

### Agreement (it/he/she)
- Use "it" (and "its", "their") for impersonal objects: tables, organizations, agents
- Use "he" and "she" for people
- If Alice is an example agent, refer to her as "she" not "it"

---

## 2. ARTICLES, DETERMINERS, AND DEFINITE DESCRIPTIONS

- Over-specified definite descriptions are ungrammatical:
  - "the Figure" ✓ or "Figure 3" ✓ — NOT "the Figure 3" ✗
- "Literature" evokes Homer and Shakespeare; "The literature" is better for CS papers

---

## 3. PREPOSITIONS

Choose carefully:
- Ancestor **of**, not to
- Beside ≠ besides — choose carefully
- Called, not called **as**
- Centered **on**, not around
- Focused **on**, not around
- Combining together — would you combine separately? Drop "together"
- Compliance **of**
- Comply **with**, not to
- "Comprises of" → use "comprises" or "consists of"
- Consider, not consider **about**
- Cooperating together — same as "combining together"; drop "together"
- Discuss, not discuss **about**
- Emphasize, NOT emphasize **on**
- Normalize X **to**, not on
- "It seems that" can be as effective as "It seems to me that"
- Avoid prepositions when possible; "for" and "or" sometimes allow multiple interpretations

---

## 4. WORDS AND PHRASES TO AVOID

### Absolutely Forbidden
1. **Slashes** (e.g., "scientists/researchers") — indicates careless thought; does the slash mean and, or, or association?
2. **And/or** — "is it and or or?"
3. **Pronouns** overuse — referent isn't always clear to reader; use names where possible
4. **His/her; he/she** — use "his or her", "he or she", or plurals
5. **They/them for singular** — OK if no ambiguity, but can be confusing
6. **etc.** — carelessness of thought; use "A, B, and so on" if needed
7. **"And so on and so forth"** — just "and so on" suffices
8. **Though** at beginning of sentence — use "although" instead
9. **He/she for an artifact** (e.g., an agent) — use "it" instead
10. **"It" for a person** — if Alice is an example agent, refer to her as "she"
11. **cf or c.f.** — people confuse with e.g.; just avoid
12. **Ad hoc** — two words, don't hyphenate

### Content-Free Words
- **Actually, basically, really** — suggest rest isn't actual/basic/real
- **Essentially** (in most uses)
- **Main, mainly** (when content-free)
- **Kind of, sort of** — meaningless
- **Relatively** — vague comparison ("this problem is relatively easy" — compared to what?)
- **Very** (Mark Twain) — weakening, not strengthening
- **At this point in time** — just say "now" or omit
- **Issue** (Lyn Dupre) — usually content-free

### Wrong Usage
- **Feel** as in "we feel that..." — use "we believe" or omit
- **Believe** about others — "researchers believe" → "researchers claim"
- **Consistency** when you mean **uniformity** — in CS, consistency means logical consistency
- **Different than** → "different from"
- **Lesser than** → "less than" (OK: "the lesser of the two evils")
- **Have to** → "must" in formal writing
- **Have** and **do** → use more meaningful verbs ("the agent does an action" → "the agent acts"; "we have a definition" → "we define")
- **While** when you mean **whereas** (while = concurrent)
- **As** when you mean **whereas** (fine for: "As remarked above, foo is bar")
- **Little** vs **a little** — nearly opposites!
- **Few** vs **a few** — "Few people attended" ≈ almost none; "A few people attended" = at least some; "Quite a few" = a lot
- **Called as** or **considered as** — just "called" or "considered"
- **Simple as** → **as simple as** (need two copies of "as")
- **Some agent** → **an agent** ("some" conveys vagueness)
- **There is/has been** at start — virtually meaningless; restructure the sentence
- **Fitted** when you mean **fit for** or **suitable** — "fitted" is what a tailor does
- **Improvise** when you mean **improve**
- **Monotonous** when you mean **monotonic** — monotonous means boring; monotonic is a math property
- **Implies/entails** — technical terms in CS; use with care; most inferences are not deductions
- **Deduce** — Arthur Conan Doyle's usage was incorrect; "inference" is more general; almost no natural inference is a deduction
- **System** — always specify which system; just about anything might be a "system"
- **Alternate** vs **alternative** — alternate = changing back and forth; alternative = choice
- **Keep** vs **put** — distinct meanings; choose carefully

### Specific Verbs
- Use specific verbs instead of general ones
- "Bob performs an action" → "Bob acts"
- "Alice obtained a high rank" → "Alice ranked at the top"
- Avoid stative verbs like "is/are" — use "become", "arise", "occur"
- Replace "holds" with "makes" where appropriate

### Gerunds
- Avoid in compound nouns: NOT "service locating"
- USE "service location" or "locating services"
- Acceptable exceptions: extremely routine phrases like "resource sharing"

### Match Singulars/Plurals
- For individual agent: "it"; for many: "they"
- "This module ensures" ✓; "These modules ensure" ✓
- "Each" and "every" take singulars — "each agents" ✗
- Singular for plural: "commitments is a means" ✗ → "commitments are a means" ✓

### Other
- **Also** — fine word, but not in every sentence
- **On** when "upon" is better — reduces copies of the common word "on"
- **Lots of** → "several" in formal writing; don't say "several" if you mean one or two
- **Get** → "obtain"
- **Firstly, secondly** → "first, second"
- **Furthermore** → "further"
- **Faculty** — a professor is not "a faculty"; faculty = entire body of teachers, or a capability
- **Allow** unless you mean allow — usually means "enable" or "facilitate"
- Words singular despite ending in -s: **semantics, pragmatics, pathos, ethos, kudos, bona fides**
- **Standard names** (SQL, XML, RDF) — use only as modifier ("an SQL query"), never standalone ("an SQL")
- Avoid unnecessary prepositions: "for" and "or" can be ambiguous; use precise relationship words

### Words to Treat Uniformly
Use consistently within any document (no hard rule):
- Life cycle / lifecycle
- Health care / healthcare

---

## 5. SPELLINGS & NON-WORDS

### Words Often Misspelled
- Ambiguous, Commitment/committed, Occurrence/occurred
- Omit/omitted, Opportunity, Pseudo
- Referrer (HTTP standard has "referer" — sic)
- Succinct, Supersede, Weird

### Mass Nouns (Never Plural)
- advice, code (software), evidence, following, information
- jargon (not jargons), noise (not noises), people (if you mean persons/users)
- research, software, traffic (not traffics)
- NOT "a software" or "three softwares" ✗
- USE "software module" or "three software modules" ✓

### Common Non-Words and Errors
- **Ad hoc** — two words, no hyphen
- **Adverse** ≠ **averse**
- **Advice** (noun) ≠ **advise** (verb)
- **Aide** (person) ≠ **aid** (help)
- **Alongwith** → "along with"
- **Alot** → "a lot"
- **Alright** → "all right"
- **Atleast** → "at least"
- **Binded** → "bound" (in most technical settings)
- **Bottleneck** — one word, don't split
- **Cannot** — one word (not(can) vs can(not))
- **Complexer** → "more complex"
- **Conjuncting** → "conjoining"
- **Cost** ≠ **price** — the difference is profit
- **Criteria** is plural (criterion is singular)
- **Duplicity** ≠ **duplication** — different meanings
- **Exhaustive** ≠ **exhausting** — different meanings
- **Framework** — one word
- **"From the scratch"** → "from scratch"
- **Id/id** → "ID" or "identifier" (unless Freudian)
- **Lead** vs **led** — "led" is past tense
- **Limited** — nearly everything is limited; say "short", "small", "few" instead
- **Loose** vs **lose**
- **Middleman** — one word
- **Onto** — not a word except as a math function
- **Parallely** → "in parallel"
- **Phenomena** is plural (phenomenon is singular)
- **Prepone** — not the opposite of postpone
- **"Request for"** as verb — wrong ("Bob requests for a quote" ✗; "Bob requests a quote" ✓)
- **Righteous** ≠ **right**
- **Splitted** → "split"
- **Thereby** ≠ **therefore**
- **Throughout** — one word
- **Tiresome** ≠ **tiring**
- **Updation** — not a word
- **Upto** → "up to"
- **Uptil** → "until"
- **Utilize** → "use"

---

## 6. EDITING & FORMATTING

### Notes on Writing
- Be willing to reorganize and rewrite large parts; don't get attached to phrasing
- Spell check the whole document, then proofread (don't offload this to readers/reviewers)
- Get other students to comment on your work before submission
- Reusing prose: OK between external submission and internal document (thesis, TR); not OK for two concurrent external submissions
- When rewriting for a new audience, rewrite the motivation even if the technical framework is reused
- Acknowledge financial support; ask advisor for grant IDs
- In acknowledgments, spell names correctly with given and last names; don't thank coauthors

### Word Processing
- Use LaTeX and BibTeX for any serious writing
- Use the target conference's style; ACM has a fussy bibliography checker that catches errors
- Overleaf: change main document name (not default main.tex); use latest TeX Live version
- Don't include standard styles (ACM, IEEE) in Overleaf projects — they're part of the distribution
- Clear all warnings; remaining warnings only acceptable if caused by a required incompatible style
- Clone Overleaf project to local folder as a backup
- Always include title, author name, and date on the title page
- Number all pages (bottom center); add back if official style removes them until final submission

### Figures & Tables
- **Table captions at top**, figure captions at bottom
- Don't have a caption within the figure itself (risk when including separate figure files)
- Name figure files systematically; match file name to internal LaTeX label
- Captions in **sentence case** (first letter uppercase, rest lowercase), end with period
- Long captions to explain figures are OK, though explanations usually go in main text
- Always refer to figures from main text
- Simple line-drawings; avoid clutter, shaded boxes (too industrial/presentation-like)
- Same typeface in figures as in main paper (Times works well)
- Use 9--10pt for text in figures (main text is 10--12pt)
- Draw figures 3.25in wide (two-column) or 5.5in wide (Springer LNCS)
- Color is fine but ensure grayscale readability; consider colorblind readers
- Use color to highlight relationships, but don't rely on it in text ("the green box")

### Capitalization
- Capitalize: Section, Figure, Table, Chapter, Algorithm, Protocol when referring to a specific one
  - "Figure 4 illustrates..." ✓
  - "the following figures show..." ✓ (lowercase)
- Section/subsection titles: capitalize all important words
- Paragraph headings: sentence case, end with period
- Discipline names: lowercase preferred ("computer science" not "Computer Science")
- Words to capitalize carefully: Internet, Web, eBay, BERT, Bayes, Bayesian, Boolean

### Numbers
- Use words for numbers ≤ 10 in text
- Use numerals for numbers > 10
- Numbers ≥ 1,000: use commas (1,000 not 1000)
- Years: no commas (2024 not 2,024)
- Don't begin sentence with numeral
- Don't spell out large numbers (not "one hundred fifty seven agents")

### Lists
- Oxford comma: "A, B, and C" ✓ (not "A, B and C" unless B and C are one unit)
- Two or more items required
- End all items with periods (preferred) or none — be consistent
- Treat all items alike in capitalization

### Whitespace and Punctuation
- Space before open parenthesis/bracket, not after
- No space before close parenthesis/bracket; space or punctuation after
- Space after comma, colon, period, semicolon; none before them
- Space before citations: "text [3]" not "text[3]"

### Footnotes
- Don't use footnotes; decide if it's worth stating in main text
- If you must: don't place superscript just before comma/period (US usage)
- If you must: don't place superscript just after a space or line break

### Quotes and Terms
- When introducing a new term, italicize it; don't use quotes
- Fewer quoted terms is better
- Closing single quote (') for apostrophe — opening quote is NOT an apostrophe
- US usage: periods and commas go inside quotes: ``this.'' and ``this,''

### Contractions
- Don't use "we'll," "I'll," "we've" (not even in drafts)
- For formal work, avoid "don't," "doesn't," "can't," "won't"
- Never use "u" or "ur" in any writing

### Sentence Beginnings
- Don't begin a sentence with:
  - A lowercase letter (work in another word: "The serviceProvider field refers to...")
  - A numeral
  - A citation
  - A bracket or parenthesis
- Author names with particles (van, de): capitalize at sentence start ("Van Riemsdijk et al. show...")

### Formulas and Notation
- Keep subscripts simple; don't over-complicate notation
- For in-text formulas, keep closing parentheses on the same line as the rest
- Use display modes (\[ \]) for large formulas with multiple subscripts

### Emphasis
- Use emphasis fonts (italics, bold) only for a few words or phrases
- When a whole sentence is parenthetical, the period goes within the parentheses

### Consistency
- Item lists: capitalize all or none consistently
- End list items all with periods or all without

---

## 7. SECTION STRUCTURE

- Section should have 0 subsections or ≥ 2 subsections
- Item lists should have ≥ 2 entries
- Document nodes: 0 children or ≥ 2 children

---

## 8. LaTeX-SPECIFIC

- En-dash: `--` (for ranges: 11--23); em-dash: `---` (for parenthetical)
- Quotes: `` `correct' `` not `"wrong"`
- Use `~` (tie) before `\ref`: `Section~\ref{sec-foo}`, `Figure~\ref{fig-foo}`
- Don't hardcode reference numbers; always use `\ref`
- Avoid "the following figures" or "the above figures" — LaTeX may place floats differently
- Use `\texttt{...}` or `\textsf{...}` for code-like text (textsf is narrower, typesets better)
- Use `\url{}` for URLs and URL-like snippets (handles line breaks)
- Don't use math fonts for multi-letter identifiers: `$FP$` shows gap → use `\emph{FP}` or `\textit{FP}`
- For identifiers with numerals: `$A_1$` and `$A_2$`
- For multi-word math identifiers: `$\textrm{ABC}_1$` or `$\textit{ABC}_1$`
- For subscripts in normal text: `ABC$_1$`
- Use `\mathrm{}` for multi-letter subscripts: `$Q_{\mathrm{FP}}$`
- Use `\[ \]` or display modes for large formulas
- Figure file names: match internal LaTeX label; use English words separated by hyphens

---

## 9. REFERENCES (BibTeX)

### Setup
- Use BibTeX (or biblatex/biber)
- Place own bib entries in a separate file named after yourself (e.g., Fardin.bib)
- Don't copy entries from advisor's bib file — duplicates generate warnings and are hard to maintain
- Don't hardcode bibliography path; use BIBINPUTS environment variable
- Default to fullname references: `\usepackage[square]{natbib}` and `\bibliographystyle{plainnat}`

### Entry Format
- Use correct entry types: @book, @article, @inproceedings, etc.
- Use braces `{ }` for string fields, not double quotes
- Use bare numbers for numeric fields (year, volume, number) — no braces or quotes
- Use three-letter month symbols (jan, feb) — let BibTeX expand as appropriate
- Define and use symbols for common series (e.g., LNCS)

### Author Names
- Full first names: "George B. Shaw" not "G.B. Shaw" or "George Bernard Shaw" if known by full middle name
- End each initial with a period
- Multiple authors: `{First1 M1. Last1 and First2 M2. Last2}` — use "and" not commas
- Suffixes: see examples like "Petrie, Jr." in advisor's bib files

### Titles and Capitalization
- Title case for booktitle and journal fields
- BibTeX auto-lowercases article/chapter titles; protect words with braces: `{Internet}`, `{Web}`, `{BERT}`
- After colon in title, capitalize next word: `{Life on the {Internet}: A Brief Report}`
- After question mark, protect next word: `{Life on the {Internet}? {An} Impossible Idea}`
- Don't enclose entire title in double braces (prevents BibTeX from changing case)

### Proceedings and Publications
- Remove redundant info from DBLP (dates, locations in booktitle)
- Shorten: "Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Foo (Foo 2022)" → "Proceedings of the Conference on Foo (Foo)"
- Use address field for conference location (more informative than publisher location)
- Supply editor for collections; publisher for collections and books
- Short publisher names; city only for well-known cities ("Berlin" not "Berlin, Germany")

### Required Fields
- Supply page numbers; also articleno and numpages when available
- Supply DOI if available; if not, ISBN (for books) or URL
- If DOI is known, exclude URL and ISBN

### Freezing
- For final publication, download the .bbl file and include its contents in the LaTeX source
- Freezes bibliography even if bib files change later

---

## 10. ORIGINALITY & QUALITY

### Originality of Presentation
- Papers must be original in presentation
- Paraphrase others' work; don't quote verbatim (purposes differ, styles clash)
- Quotations acceptable only for especially pithy sayings or specious claims you will rebut
- Not acceptable to simply reorder bullet items or make minor grammatical changes (e.g., active→passive)
- Credit originators with citations; for recent topics, cite originators directly; for well-known topics, cite surveys/textbooks

### Originality of Content
- Research papers must be original in content
- Make reasonable effort to determine if others had the same idea
- Building on others' work is expected — describe it in your own words (paraphrase)

### Value Added
- Research writing is more than narrative of steps taken
- Consider the contribution: original scientific content, novel synthesis, or new analysis
- If original content: what problem does it solve, what phenomenon does it explain?
- If novel synthesis: what new perspective does it motivate?

### Quality of Presentation
- Organization and quality of prose matter
- Spell check and proofread
- Re-read what you wrote several days later — you will find unclarities and ambiguities
- Rewrite large parts if needed (don't get attached to phrasing)
- Get peer feedback before submission

---

## 11. DRAWING TOOLS

When using external drawing tools (prefer tikz in LaTeX when possible):
- Make the grid visible to simplify alignment
- Use boxes of reasonably large size
- Align all boxes on grid lines
- Same width and height for boxes in the same column/row
- Place all connectors on connection points
- Make connection points visible; insert points on box edges as needed
- Connectors should follow grid lines
- Magnify to 400% to check alignment

## QUICK CHECKLIST FOR PAPERS

- [ ] "Related Work" not "Related Works"
- [ ] No etc., slashes, and/or in formal text
- [ ] No content-free words (actually, basically, very, relatively, etc.)
- [ ] No contractions in formal writing
- [ ] `\texttt{}` or `\textsf{}` for code/fields
- [ ] Figure captions: sentence case, at bottom, end with period
- [ ] Table captions: sentence case, at top, end with period
- [ ] No caption within the figure itself
- [ ] Figures referenced from main text
- [ ] Figure text: 9--10pt, same typeface as main paper
- [ ] Numbers ≤10 as words; ≥1,000 with commas; years without commas
- [ ] No past/future tense for paper structure ("Section 5 presents...")
- [ ] No "however" joining clauses with comma
- [ ] Active voice throughout
- [ ] Citations include author names
- [ ] No slash constructions (and/or, scientists/researchers)
- [ ] Comparators specify comparison ("faster than X")
- [ ] "That" (restrictive) vs "which" (non-restrictive) used correctly
- [ ] Hyphens only for compound modifiers ("run-time error" but "at run time")
- [ ] En-dashes for ranges, em-dashes for parentheticals
- [ ] Space before citations: `text [3]`
- [ ] Don't begin sentences with citation, numeral, lowercase, or bracket
- [ ] New terms italicized, not quoted
- [ ] All sections have 0 or ≥2 subsections
- [ ] All lists have ≥2 items
- [ ] List formatting consistent (capitalization, periods)
- [ ] No footnotes
- [ ] Emphasis (bold/italics) used sparingly
- [ ] BibTeX: full author names, braces for strings, protected capitalizations
- [ ] BibTeX: DOI supplied if available
- [ ] Spell check complete; then proofread
- [ ] Peer feedback obtained
